# Respondents {#sec-respondents}

`sc_posterior()` summarizes individual respondents: what the fitted model says about one
respondent's tastes, given that respondent's characteristics and choices.

```{r}
#| label: r-setup
#| cache: false
library(sconjoint)
fits <- getOption("sconjoint.fits", "fits")
gs <- sc_load(file.path(fits, "gs_q3.rds"))
if (is.null(gs)) stop("This chapter needs the saved fit gs_q3.rds; see the installation chapter.")
```

## Posterior

Before any choices, the model predicts a respondent's tastes from their characteristics: normal,
with mean $\mu(Z_i)$ and covariance $\Lambda\Lambda^\top$. This is the *prior*. Bayes' rule
combines the prior with the respondent's choices into the *posterior*, an updated distribution of
that respondent's tastes at the fitted parameters.

With thirteen tasks, the choices carry little information. The posterior stays close to the prior,
and its mean is pulled toward the mean of respondents with the same characteristics. It is a
prediction of the respondent's tastes, not a measurement of them. Only with many tasks does the
posterior concentrate around the respondent's own tastes.

## Democracy experiment

For fold states, `sc_posterior()` uses the fit that did not train on the respondent's choices. A
contrast is a named vector or a matrix with one row per contrast.

```{r}
#| label: r-gs
partisans <- which(gs$data$groups$PL == 1)
cp <- matrix(1, 1, 1, dimnames = list("co-partisan", "diff_respParty"))
post <- sc_posterior(gs, respondents = partisans[1:6], contrasts = cp)
post
round(post$contrasts[, c("prior_mean", "prior_sd", "mean", "sd", "lower", "upper",
                         "prob_positive")], 2)
```

The first two respondents have similar priors, a co-partisan taste of about 1.4 and 1.1 with a
standard deviation of 0.87. After their thirteen choices, the first respondent's posterior mean
rises to 1.75 and the second's falls to 0.27. `prob_positive` is the posterior probability that the
co-partisan taste is positive. The posterior standard deviations are about three quarters of the
prior ones. `history = 0` returns the prior:

```{r}
#| label: r-history0
round(sc_posterior(gs, respondents = partisans[1:2], contrasts = cp, history = 0)$contrasts[,
  c("prior_mean", "mean", "sd")], 2)
```

## Counting posterior means

The share of respondents with a positive posterior mean is not an estimate of the preference share.
Posterior means are shrunk toward the prior means, so they spread less than tastes do, and their
signs follow the prior. The population quantities average over each respondent's whole taste
distribution instead.

```{r}
#| label: r-count
all_pl <- sc_posterior(gs, respondents = partisans, contrasts = cp)
law <- sc_fitted_law(gs, "diff_respParty", w = "PL")
rbind(
  "posterior means" = c(sd = sd(all_pl$contrasts$mean), positive = mean(all_pl$contrasts$mean > 0)),
  "fitted law" = c(sd = attr(law, "summary")[["sd"]], positive = attr(law, "summary")[["share_positive"]]))
```

The 1,377 posterior means spread less than the fitted law. The share with a positive posterior mean
is neither the fitted share of 83.3% nor the corrected share of 82.5% in @sec-gs. Posterior
summaries also condition on the fitted parameters, so they carry no sampling uncertainty from the
fit.

## Long panels

With many tasks per respondent, the posterior can learn individual tastes. The paper shows this
with a 30-task experiment. The code below simulates one with known tastes: 200 respondents, 30
tasks each, three coded features, one taste factor and a position effect. `sc_posterior()` also
takes fitted parameters directly, as a list with `mu`, `kappa`, `loading` and `omega`.

```{r}
#| label: r-sim
set.seed(30)
n <- 200; n_tasks <- 30; p <- 3
X <- matrix(sample(c(-1, 0, 1), n * n_tasks * p, TRUE), n * n_tasks, p,
            dimnames = list(NULL, c("party", "college", "experience")))
id <- rep(seq_len(n), each = n_tasks)
mu <- cbind(party = rnorm(n, 0.8, 0.3), college = rnorm(n, 0.3, 0.2), experience = 0.2)
L <- matrix(c(0.9, 0.4, 0.2), p, 1)
beta <- mu + rnorm(n) %o% L[, 1]
omega <- 0.3; kappa <- 0.1
y <- rbinom(n * n_tasks, 1, plogis(kappa + rowSums(X * beta[id, ]) + sqrt(omega) * rnorm(n)[id]))
dat <- sc_data(y, X, id)
par_true <- list(mu = mu, kappa = kappa, loading = L, omega = omega)
```

For each history (the number of first tasks conditioned on), the code computes the posterior of the
party taste and predicts the final five tasks. The parameters are the true ones, so the table shows
what the choices themselves add.

```{r}
#| label: r-learning
learn <- t(sapply(c(0, 3, 8, 15, 25), function(h) {
  newtasks <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) X[id == i, , drop = FALSE][26:30, ])
  post <- sc_posterior(par_true, dat, contrasts = c(party = 1), history = h, newtasks = newtasks)
  obs <- y[rep(seq_len(n_tasks), n) > 25]
  pr <- post$predictions$prob
  c(history = h,
    posterior_sd = median(post$contrasts$sd),
    cor_with_truth = cor(post$contrasts$mean, beta[, "party"]),
    log_loss_last5 = -mean(obs * log(pr) + (1 - obs) * log(1 - pr)))
}))
round(learn, 3)
```

As the history grows, the posterior standard deviation of the party taste falls, the posterior
means track the true tastes more closely, and predictions of the last five choices improve. With 25
earlier choices the posterior is still far from a point. Choices are noisy, and each task carries
little information about any one taste.

The default integrator (`method = "adaptive"`) centers its draws at each respondent's posterior
mode, so it stays accurate when the posterior is much narrower than the prior. The `diagnostics`
table reports each respondent's effective sample size. If it is small, increase the draws with
`nodes`.
